children: Crude and refined product futures finished mixed Tuesday while U.S. diesel futures rose sharply, as the lifting of U.S. sanctions on Russian diesel and the new tax break for on-road use of dyed diesel failed to bring down prices.
President Trump's agreement with Russia intended to increase diesel supplies is unlikely to resolve tightness in global middle-distillate markets,
, and trucking companies generally lack access to dyed diesel or avoid using it because of the associated recordkeeping burden, transportation technology firm Breakthrough said.

Analysts at ING said the proposed volumes would do little to resolve tightness and that the market remains skeptical of a proposed Russia-Ukraine ceasefire covering energy infrastructure after Russia continued to strike Ukrainian energy targets.
Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia intercepted more missiles and drones launched by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis, and the Saudi Aramco (
) headquarters was hit in the latest attacks.

President Trump accused the Houthis of intentionally increasing global oil prices through their strikes on Saudi energy infrastructure and the Riyadh airport in recent days and suggested the attacks were timed to influence global markets before the U.S. midterm elections.

Oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz fell sharply toward the end of last week as attacks on tankers increased, according to preliminary data from Kpler data, as confirmed flows slumped to 2M bbl/day on Saturday from 6.7M bbl/day on Friday and 22.8M bbl/day on Thursday.

OPEC also lowered its ​forecast for 2026 oil demand growth for a sixth straight month to 180K bbl/day from 380K bbl/day previously and raised its forecast for next year to 2.55M bbl/day from 2.36M bbl/day, citing the need for the world to rebuild inventories depleted during the Iran war.

"While the day-to-day headlines constantly move, the overarching picture in the Persian Gulf has been little changed throughout the past three months," Raymond James analyst Pavel Molchanov said in a note.
